solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); the blog's row for 19ac left its clue-number cell blank (the row sits directly between 17/11 and 21ac, its clue text matches 19ac's verbatim, and SINGLET's 7 letters match 19ac's grid length) — number supplied

clue.text: Old racing driver takes the Eye to be a means of entrapment

indicators.note: Something that takes another in receives it inside itself, so the short piece goes within the name.

blocks.note: John Cobb, the British driver who held the land speed record in the 1930s and 1940s.
Private Eye, where this crossword appears, writes of itself as 'we'.

explanation.surface: A retired racing driver reckons the magazine is out to catch him.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion lands between the two Bs of the driver's surname. Cobb was killed in 1952 attempting the water speed record on Loch Ness.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobweb is the spider's trap, spun across a gap to catch whatever blunders into it.

clue.text: Nowt wrong with Bush – mad to ignore a sign of rejection

indicators.note: Something wrong is not as it should be, so the letters end up in an order that is not theirs.
To ignore something is to leave it out, so the letter named never joins the mix.

blocks.note: Nowt is northern English for nothing; the four letters go into the mix.
The name is taken as letters.
Three more letters.
This A is taken out of MAD, leaving MD.

explanation.surface: There was nothing wrong with Bush, mad though he was to overlook a warning.
explanation.walkthrough: Which Bush is never settled, because the name is wanted only for its letters. 'Nowt wrong' reads as a verdict and is really two instructions plus the first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The thumbs-down is the gesture that condemns, still given to mean no when something is turned down.

clue.text: see 24dn.
Having an erection finish without definitive climax is incorrigible

indicators.note: Without is used in its old sense of outside, so the piece before it closes round the letter after it.
A climax is the high point at the end, so the word gives up its final letter.

blocks.note: A man with an erection is hard.
To finish is to end.
The last letter of DEFINITIVE.

explanation.surface: A man with an erection finishes before the decisive moment and will not be told.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like the everyday sense, lacking, which would take letters away; here it puts one inside instead. Incorrigible and hardened meet in the hardened criminal, past reforming.
explanation.definitionFit: A hardened offender is set in their ways and beyond correcting, which is what incorrigible means.

clue.text: Neutralise rotten lay

blocks.note: Food gone rotten is off.
To lay something down is to set it down.

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a lover's performance as a rotten lay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' reads as the crude noun the surface wants; the wordplay needs the verb, to put something down. Three plain words, none of them announcing that anything is being built.
explanation.definitionFit: To offset something is to counterbalance it until its effect cancels out, which is neutralising it.

clue.text: No alibi? Got to get fixed charge

indicators.note: Something fixed has been taken apart and put back together, so the letters come back in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: These ten letters are rearranged.

explanation.surface: A suspect with no alibi has been stitched up with a charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark falls in the middle, where the surface is asking after the suspect's alibi, so it does not look like the end of anything. 'Charge' is a duty, not a police one.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge is a responsibility laid on someone, the thing they are obliged to see to.

clue.text: see 25dn.
Last out conflict with Trump – arse has gone "valiant"

indicators.note: Letters put out are turned out of their places and come back in another order.
What has gone is no longer there, so those letters are taken off the name.

blocks.note: The letters of LAST rearranged.
A conflict is a war.
The name is taken as letters.
A rump is a backside, and RUMP comes out of TRUMP, leaving T.

explanation.surface: A feud with Trump lasts to the end, the arse departs, and someone is called valiant.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the arse off Trump is the joke and the mechanism at once: four letters of his name go and one is left. The quotation marks let the praise be someone else's.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalwart means sturdy and resolute, standing firm where others give way, which is the claim 'valiant' makes.

clue.text: Hillary or Bill, possibly for health reforms

definitions.note: The Clintons are an example of the relation rather than a synonym for it, which is what 'possibly' admits.

indicators.note: To reform something is to shape it again, so the letters take a new shape.

blocks.note: These nine letters are rearranged.

explanation.surface: Hillary or Bill Clinton campaigning for changes to health care.
explanation.walkthrough: Health reform was Hillary Clinton's own project as First Lady, so the phrase reads as policy rather than as letters. Each Clinton is the other's, which is why either name will do.
explanation.definitionFit: Your other half is your spouse, and the Clintons are each other's, so either is an instance of one.

clue.text: Trump, apparently unfussy sexually, to leave on time

definitions.note: Trump is offered as a specimen rather than a synonym, and 'apparently' marks the verdict as the magazine's.

blocks.note: Someone bisexual is not fussy about a partner's sex.
To leave is to go.
T is the standard abbreviation for time.

explanation.surface: Trump is said to be easy-going about sex and keen to leave punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' does the work a question mark usually does, offering Trump as one of these rather than the meaning of the word. This appeared a fortnight before the 2016 election.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigot is someone stubbornly prejudiced against a whole group of people, which is what the clue accuses Trump of being.

clue.text: see 17ac.
Lives with SNP leader, wearing forlorn sack

indicators.note: A leader goes at the head, so the word gives its first letter.
What you wear goes round the outside of you, so the word after it closes over the letters before it.

blocks.note: Forlorn and dismal are both dejected.
He lives is he is.
The first letter of SNP, the Scottish National Party.

explanation.surface: Somebody shares a life with the SNP leader, dressed in a sad-looking sack.
explanation.walkthrough: The garment reading of 'sack' is the trap, and it is supported by 'wearing', which is not describing clothes at all. Nicola Sturgeon led the SNP in 2016; the party gives only its initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the sack is being put out of a job, and a dismissal is the act of putting someone out of one.

clue.text: Ex-football star geezer is match attendant

blocks.note: George Best, the Manchester United and Northern Ireland winger, who died in 2005.
Geezer is British slang for a bloke.

explanation.surface: An old football star and some bloke are on duty at the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match attendant' points at a steward at a football ground, which is where the surface has already put us. The match is a marriage and the attendant stands beside the groom.
explanation.definitionFit: The best man attends the groom at a wedding, and a match is a marriage.

clue.text: Two Democrats implicated in email set fiasco – a troublesome area

indicators.note: Someone implicated in a mess is caught up in it, so these letters are mixed in with the rest.
A fiasco is a shambles, so the letters are left in disarray.

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for Democrat, so two of them give DD.
Eight more letters for the mix.

explanation.surface: Two Democrats are caught up in a disaster over a set of emails.
explanation.walkthrough: Hillary Clinton's private email server was the running scandal of the 2016 campaign, so the surface has a ready-made story to lean on. What comes out is a region, not a row.
explanation.definitionFit: The Middle East has been the world's most persistently war-torn region, which is the trouble the definition means.

clue.text: Extra-cheap housing for air-tube

indicators.note: A house holds what is inside it, so the answer is being held inside the words beside it.

blocks.note: Sitting in exTRA-CHEAp, running straight through the hyphen.

explanation.surface: Bargain-basement accommodation.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen is there to be read through, and the eye obligingly stops at it. Hidden answers often straddle punctuation for exactly that reason.
explanation.definitionFit: The trachea is the windpipe, the tube carrying air from the throat down to the lungs.

clue.text: Coach to go in the container provided?

definitions.text: Coach to go in the container provided?

blocks.note: Read straight, a coach setting off on a journey; read the setter's way, teaching an animal to relieve itself.
Not a crate the coach is loaded into, but the tray put down indoors for the purpose.

explanation.surface: A coach is loaded into the shipping container laid on for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' is the nursery euphemism and 'coach' is the verb, to train. House means to contain as well, which is the extra wink in the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To housetrain an animal is to teach it to relieve itself indoors only where you want it to, in the tray provided.

clue.text: (&11ac.) Do fanciful broadcast with "wild tomboy", Theresa May?

definitions.note: May is an example, as the question mark admits: the phrase was fastened to her in 2016 and she kept it.

indicators.note: To broadcast is to scatter seed in all directions, so the letters are strewn into a new order.

blocks.note: Ten letters for the mix.
Ten more, making twenty.

explanation.surface: A fanciful broadcast about a wild tomboy asks whether Theresa May was one.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Clarke was filmed in July 2016, not realising the camera was running, calling the incoming prime minister a bloody difficult woman. 'Wild' sits inside the quotation marks so it looks like part of that broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarke's unguarded description stuck to Theresa May, who then used it of herself, so the phrase names her.

clue.text: Bricks tossed over state Chancellor

indicators.note: Something tossed is thrown about and lands any way up, so the letters come down in a new order.
What goes over something covers it, so the rearranged letters close round the piece that follows.

blocks.note: Six letters to be rearranged.
MA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Massachusetts.

explanation.surface: Bricks are lobbed across a state line at the Chancellor.
explanation.walkthrough: Otto von Bismarck was the first Chancellor of the German Empire, and Bismarck is the capital of North Dakota, which is what puts a state in the clue at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Bismarck held the office of Chancellor for nineteen years, having made the empire he then ran.

clue.text: When Clinton might triumph over Dow Jones central collapse

indicators.note: In a down entry the piece written over another sits above it, so the autumn goes on top.
The central letter of a word is the single one at its middle.

blocks.note: American presidential elections are held in the fall, so that is when Clinton's win would have come.
The Dow Jones share index, taken as letters.
The middle letter of JONES.

explanation.surface: Clinton's victory arrives just as the New York market caves in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall' is the American word for autumn, and the election falls in November. With the Dow Jones already in the clue, 'collapse' reads as a market crash rather than as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall down is to collapse, dropping in a heap where you stood.

clue.text: Squeal "rent undergarment!"

blocks.note: To squeal on someone is to sing, informing on them.
A property rented out is let.

explanation.surface: An outraged shriek that somebody's underwear has been torn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' reads as torn, the past participle of rend, which is what the shriek is about; the wordplay wants the landlord's sense. Grassing someone up is singing on both sides of the Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless vest, worn under a shirt or by boxers and runners.

clue.text: Right embroiled in stink, leader having quit (depression)

indicators.note: Someone embroiled in a mess is caught up inside it, so the letter goes within the word that follows.
The leader is the letter at the front, and having quit it is gone, so the word starts one letter later.

blocks.note: A stink is a stench; its leading S has quit, leaving TENCH.
R is the standard abbreviation for right.

explanation.surface: The right is caught up in a scandal after its leader resigns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' and 'leader' both pull towards politics, and a stink is what a scandal gets called, so all three words look like the same story. The definition is the one in brackets at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A trench is a long hollow cut into the ground, so it is a depression in a surface.

clue.text: Balls once associated with such capers, wielding canes left and right

definitions.text: Balls once associated with such capers
definitions.note: The definition describes the dance by where it was danced rather than naming it, which is what 'such' points at.

indicators.note: To wield something is to swing it about, so the letters beside it are thrown into a new order.

blocks.note: Five letters for the mix.
L for left and R for right, the standard abbreviations.

explanation.surface: Ed Balls capering about, swinging canes to left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls, out of Parliament since 2015, was on Strictly Come Dancing as this was published, which is what 'Balls' and 'capers' are trading on. The Lancers is a Victorian quadrille danced in sets of five figures.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lancers was a standard dance of the Victorian ballroom, so balls of that era were given over to such capers.

clue.text: Star group's messy break-up? About time

indicators.note: A break-up leaves the pieces scattered, so the letters come apart and re-form.
Letters set about something close round it, so the scattered five take the sixth in.

blocks.note: Five letters to be rearranged.
T is the standard abbreviation for time.

explanation.surface: A band splits acrimoniously, and not before time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star group' reads as a band and the break-up as the split that ends one, so the stars look like celebrities. 'About time' is the remark a fan would add, and it hands over a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A star system is a star with everything bound to it, so a group of stars held together is one.

clue.text: Nick happened to go wrong around middle of March

indicators.note: Something that goes wrong ends up out of order, so the letters are rearranged.
Letters set around another take it in among them.
The middle of a word is the letter standing at its centre.

blocks.note: Eight letters for the mix.
The middle letter of MARCH.

explanation.surface: Something went badly wrong in the middle of March.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' opens the sentence looking like a man's name, which is why the capital letter tells you nothing. It is the police verb, and a five-letter month has one letter at its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick someone is British slang for arresting them, which is what the police do when they apprehend a suspect.

clue.text: (& 3dn.) Act the tosser with press, as Schwarzenegger would once do

definitions.note: The definition is a clause describing the action rather than naming it, so it stands in for a verb phrase.

blocks.note: To pump is to work something up and down, the action a tosser is named for.
To press clothes is to iron them.

explanation.surface: Making a fool of yourself in front of the newspapers, as Schwarzenegger used to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tosser' is the British insult and 'press' the newspapers, so the surface is about behaving badly in public. Arnold Schwarzenegger was Mr Universe before he was an actor, and a bench press is weightlifting too.
explanation.definitionFit: To pump iron is to lift weights, which is how Schwarzenegger built the bodybuilding titles that made his name.

clue.text: Rotating instrument for flies

indicators.note: Something rotating is turned right round, so the word beside it is read backwards.

blocks.note: A Strad is a Stradivarius violin, and STRAD turned round gives the answer.

explanation.surface: A spinning gadget sold for dealing with flies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instrument' is asked to produce a specific one, and the violin is the crossword's usual answer to that. In an across entry a rotation simply reads the letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A swallow darts across a field, which is to say it flies fast and straight, so one verb stands for the other.

clue.text: (& 7dn.) Sun quite lacking, deteriorates: no time for intellectual enlightenment?

definitions.note: The definition describes the period by what it is said to have lacked rather than naming it, which is what the question mark flags.

blocks.note: With the sun altogether absent it is dark.
Something that deteriorates over time ages.

explanation.surface: Deprived of sunshine, something slowly goes downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S invites the Sun, the tabloid, which is where the jab about intellectual enlightenment lands. The Dark Ages are the centuries after Rome, named for how little was written down in them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dark Ages are the early medieval stretch when learning is said to have gone out in Europe, so they were no time for enlightenment.

clue.text: He wrote of our absurd situation: "flipping problem with a Conservative leader"

definitions.text: He wrote of our absurd situation
definitions.note: The definition describes the writer instead of naming him, which is the usual way a person's surname is defined.

indicators.note: To flip something is to turn it over, so everything gathered after it is read backwards.
A leader stands at the head of the word, so only its first letter is wanted.

blocks.note: A problem in arithmetic is a sum.
The word is taken as its own letter.
The first letter of CONSERVATIVE.

explanation.surface: A grumble in quotation marks about the blasted trouble with having a Conservative leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is the mild British swear in the surface and the turnaround in the wordplay, and it is placed so that a reader hears the swear first. Albert Camus held that life is absurd and must be lived anyway.
explanation.definitionFit: Camus built his work on the absurd, the gap between our search for meaning and a universe that offers none.

clue.text: Noel with refreshment lacking in 'bottle quality'

definitions.note: The phrase names the quality itself: bottle is nerve, and the answer is the word for going without it.

blocks.note: Noel Coward, the English playwright and songwriter.
Ice is what refreshes a drink.

explanation.surface: Noel's drink is judged short of the quality a bottle ought to have.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward wrote Private Lives and Brief Encounter, and his first name alone is enough to summon him. Bottle is British slang for nerve, which is why losing yours is losing your courage.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottle is British slang for nerve, so the quality of having none of it is cowardice.
